content: Lead(II) sulfate, also referred to as lead(II) sulphate in British English, is a chemical compound with the formula PbSO₄. It appears as a white crystalline solid or powder. This compound is also known by other names, including white lead, fast white, milk white, sulfuric acid lead salt, or anglesite. Lead(II) sulfate is commonly observed in the terminals of car batteries. It forms during the discharge process of the battery. When the battery is recharged, the lead sulfate can be converted back into metallic lead and sulfuric acid at the negative terminal, or into lead dioxide and sulfuric acid at the positive terminal. This compound is characterized by its poor solubility in water. Toxicology Lead(II) sulfate is highly toxic and poses significant health risks through inhalation, ingestion, or skin contact. It is a cumulative poison, meaning that repeated exposure can result in severe health consequences. These include anemia, kidney damage, visual impairment, and damage to the central nervous system, with children being particularly vulnerable. Certain lead salts, including lead sulfate, may also cause reproductive defects and cardiovascular disturbances. Additionally, lead sulfate is corrosive; contact with the eyes can result in severe irritation or chemical burns. Mineral Form The naturally occurring mineral form of lead(II) sulfate is known as anglesite. This mineral, with the chemical formula PbSO₄, is formed as an oxidation product of the primary lead sulfide ore, galena. Basic and Hydrogen Lead Sulfates Several basic lead sulfates are known, including compounds with the formulas PbSO₄·PbO, PbSO₄·2PbO, PbSO₄·3PbO, and PbSO₄·4PbO. These basic lead sulfates are utilized in the production of active paste for lead-acid batteries. A related mineral, leadhillite, has the formula 2PbCO₃·PbSO₄·Pb(OH)₂. At high concentrations of sulfuric acid (greater than 80%), hydrogen lead sulfate, with the formula Pb(HSO₄)₂, can form.
